newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Emerging markets regain lustre for money managers.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets regain lustre for money managers.

text.p: The world's money managers, at a "crystal ball" session here, predicted Tuesday that emerging markets would outshine the developed world in 1997 on expected inflows of U.S. cash and prospects of high liquidity and growth.
Fund managers at an international investment conference expected a reallocation of assets away from the rich world in 1997 to produce a healthy flow of funds into emerging markets.

"With very strong earnings in emerging markets, I expect them to outperform, not just catch up with, the developed world," said Arnab Banerji, chief investment officer at London's Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets, which has $5 billion under management.
"There will be a rotation out of developed markets and a reallocation of assets away from the United States into emerging markets," he told the conference.

Despite rallies in Eastern Europe and Russia and in smaller markets like Venezuela and Bangladesh, emerging markets in 1996 failed to provide the dizzying returns of 1993. But cash flows into the developing world should continue to recover in 1997, lured by prospects of lower interest rates, high domestic liquidity and high growth, money managers said.

Michael Howell, head of London's Crossborder Capital and a respected emerging market economist, said $50 billion of the world's money flew into emerging markets in 1996 -- up from $15 billion in 1995, $40 billion in 1994 and a peak of $63 billion in 1993.
"In 1997, we expect flows to be similar to this year's $50 billion," he added.
